passage:
Nilesh: You looked so calm last month. How did you handle the report, your sister's wedding shopping and the volunteering all at once?
Gargi: Honestly, I nearly didn't. On a Sunday I took a page and wrote everything I'd promised, all eight things. I stared at it. Then I told the people who needed to know: the volunteering group got “I'll skip two weeks”, my sister got “Saturdays only for the shopping”, and my manager got the report date confirmed. Then I worked through them in order, single-mindedly. It was a bit awkward saying it aloud. But nobody was angry, and nothing collapsed silently, which is what I was scared of.

qa.q: How many things did Gargi write on the page?
qa.a: Gargi wrote down all eight things, everything promised.

qa.q: What did Gargi feel about telling people what would be delayed?
qa.a: Gargi felt awkward saying it aloud, and was scared that things would collapse silently, but nobody was angry.

qa.q: What did Gargi tell the sister and the volunteering group?
qa.a: Gargi told the sister that shopping would be on Saturdays only, and told the volunteering group that Gargi would skip two weeks.

qa.q: What might Nilesh be thinking as Gargi explains?
qa.a: Nilesh is probably curious and impressed, and may be thinking of Nilesh's own overloaded list.

grounding: A wise person lists commitments, tells relevant people what will be delayed, and does each task in turn.

passage: I'm Mahima, and last Monday I saw Seema do something I'd never seen anyone do. Seema had four projects, a training day and a family function that week. Instead of frowning at all of them, Seema took a sticky note, wrote them in order and crossed off one that could wait. Then Seema walked to the manager's desk and said, “The vendor review will move to next Wednesday. Everything else stays.” A call went to the training coordinator too, and a message to a cousin about the function. After that Seema worked on one file only, phone face down. I can't say how Seema felt, but the day looked calmer than mine.

qa.q: Which task did Seema move to next Wednesday?
qa.a: Seema moved the vendor review to next Wednesday.

qa.q: How does Mahima think Seema felt that day?
qa.a: Mahima cannot be sure, but Seema looked calmer, and probably felt steadier after telling people the truth about what would wait.

qa.q: What steps did Seema take before working on a single file?
qa.a: Seema wrote the commitments in order, crossed one off, told the manager, the training coordinator and a cousin, and then put the phone face down.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt hearing that the vendor review would move?
qa.a: The manager may feel a little surprised, but honest notice at once lets the manager plan, which is better than silent failing.

grounding: A wise person lists commitments, tells relevant people what will be delayed and does each task in turn.

passage:
Monday. Sharmila, twenty-five, had a report due, a friend's wedding to help with, a course assignment and her mother's move to a new flat, all in the same fortnight. She had been silently failing at all four: late nights, half-finished slides, missed calls.
Tuesday. She wrote every commitment on one sheet and numbered them. Then she did the hard part. She told her manager Abhinav the report would come on the 18th, not the 15th, and why. She texted her friend that she could help on the wedding day but not with planning.
Following Monday. She went in order: the move on Saturday, the report on Tuesday. Abhinav said, "Thanks for telling me early." She slept properly for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What date did Sharmila tell Abhinav the report would come?
qa.a: She said the report would come on the 18th, not the 15th.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel by the following Monday?
qa.a: She felt relieved and rested, sleeping properly for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: Which steps helped Sharmila, and why?
qa.a: Listing every commitment, telling people what would be delayed and doing one thing at a time replaced silent failing with honest limits.

qa.q: How does Abhinav react to Sharmila's early message?
qa.a: Abhinav is appreciative, thanking Sharmila for the early warning, which leaves room to plan.

grounding: Shows over a week a young worker listing all commitments, telling people what will be delayed and doing one thing at a time.

passage: Madhuri, come, sit with your Periamma. You're doing too much, like your mother Sudha did at your age. When she was twenty-four, she was teaching at the school, looking after your grandfather after his surgery and helping me with my tailoring orders. She was failing quietly at all three: late to class, missing his medicines, my orders half-stitched. One night she sat at the kitchen table with a notebook and wrote everything down. The next morning she went to the headmistress and asked to drop the extra evening class for a month. She told me my orders would be late. She did his medicines first each morning, then school. Everyone was a little disappointed. Nobody was let down.

qa.q: How old was Sudha in the story?
qa.a: Sudha was twenty-four.

qa.q: What might Sudha have felt the night she sat at the kitchen table?
qa.a: She probably felt overwhelmed and guilty, failing quietly at three duties at once.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Sudha most?
qa.a: Writing everything down and then asking to drop the evening class and telling Periamma the orders would be late, so she could do one thing at a time.

qa.q: How might the headmistress have felt about Sudha's request?
qa.a: The headmistress may have been a little disappointed but likely respected Sudha for asking honestly rather than slipping further.

grounding: An elder recalls a young woman listing her commitments, telling others what would be delayed and doing one thing at a time.

passage: Chinmay, twenty-four, had ten days before his cousin Indu's wedding in Nashik, where he was in charge of the guest travel. At the same time his team's software release was due, and his landlord had given notice. On top of that, his laptop charger died on Tuesday. Stuck with a dying battery, he wrote every commitment on a paper napkin at the café. Then he made three calls. He told his lead that the release notes would be two days late. He asked Indu if an uncle could handle the airport pickups. He asked the landlord for an extra week. Everyone agreed. That night, he booked twenty train tickets, one task, done.

qa.q: What was Chinmay in charge of for the wedding?
qa.a: He was in charge of the guest travel.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel after the three calls?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved and steadier, with each person agreeing to a delay or a change.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay's approach work better than trying to do everything at once?
qa.a: Listing commitments, telling people what would slip and doing one thing at a time turned silent overload into a manageable order.

qa.q: How might Indu feel about Chinmay's request for help with pickups?
qa.a: Indu might feel reassured that the travel plans are in steady hands, even with an uncle taking the airport pickups.

grounding: Shows a worker under pressure listing his commitments, renegotiating dates and doing one thing at a time.

passage: On Sunday evening in her Bengaluru flat, Jahnavi tore a page from a notebook and wrote down everything she had promised: the manuscript edit due to the publisher on Thursday, packing for the move, Kannada class twice a week, and Darshan's pitch deck, which she had said she'd polish by Friday. Seeing it all on one page made her stomach drop. Then she numbered it. Manuscript first. Then she sent three messages. To Darshan: "I can't do the deck by Friday. I can give it a proper look next Wednesday. Is that okay, or should you ask someone else?" To her Kannada teacher: "Skipping two weeks, back on the 20th." To the landlord: "Can the move shift by a week?" On Monday she worked only on the manuscript, phone face-down until lunch. It went out on Thursday morning. Darshan had replied within an hour: "Thanks for telling me. Wednesday works."

qa.q: What did Jahnavi put first on the numbered list?
qa.a: The manuscript edit due to the publisher on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when she saw everything on one page?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed, her stomach dropped, and she became calmer once the list was numbered and the messages were sent.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling Darshan, the teacher and the landlord what would slip, then doing one thing at a time, let her finish the manuscript without quietly failing the others.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel getting the message on Sunday rather than a missed Friday?
qa.a: Darshan is relieved and grateful to know early, with time to choose between waiting and asking someone else.

grounding: Illustrates listing all commitments, telling the right people what will be delayed and working through them one at a time.
